newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says his budget will contain net tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says his budget will contain net tax cuts.

text.p: President Clinton on Tuesday disputed reports that his budget will on balance contain tax increases, saying that in fact he thought there would be a net cut in tax levels.
"I believe we have a net tax cut," Clinton told a news conference.

He said that he believed that virtually all the corporate loopholes to be closed in the budget were those that were discussed and generally agreed with the congresssional leadership during the budget negotiations.
He said that so far both sides had toned down their rhetoric and that "on balance I am quite hopeful" that balanced budget agreement can be reached.

While emphasizing the importance of reaching a balanced budget agreement, Clinton also reiterated his opposition to a Republican proposal to amend the Constitution to require a balanced federal budget.
The proposal would put the government at risk of having to take measures that are "counterproductive" during times of potential economic crises, the president said.
"When you amend the Constitution, you do it forever," he said. "No one can foresee the circumstances that will come a generation from now or 50 years from now or even 10 years from now."

Asked his view about proposals to privatize Social Security partially by having contributors place a portion of their payroll taxes into individual accounts for investment, Clinton said he could not support such an option without reviewing it further.
He pointed out that a federally appointed advisory panel reviewing the Social Security system could not reach agreement on options for overhauling the program.
Clinton, however, stressed the need to make small changes to lengthen the life of the Social Security trust fund.

"If we start now, we can make modest changes that won't be too burdensome to anybody (who) will secure Social Security for another 50 years and I think that's what we ought to be doing," Clinton said.
Clinton also told reporters that his budget will contain a proposed homeowners capital gains exemption, but that a broader capital gains cut was not a priority.
"The capital gains issue has never been a particular high priority for me because I've never seen it demonstrated as a big engine of economic growth overall," he said.
But he said he wanted to hold down the rhetoric and would present his budget and that "we need to meet each other in good faith."
"This and all other issues can best be resolved by an early attempt to work through to a balanced budget agreement," he added.
